intro: The piano begins by accompanying the strings, planting huge chords beneath their D♭-major melody. Tchaikovsky spends that famous tune in the introduction, then builds the rest of the movement from other songs.

sections.label: Intro · Piano chords beneath the strings
sections.mNote: Horns announce the opening; strings sing in D♭ major

sections.label: A · The piano’s Ukrainian tune
sections.mNote: The Allegro begins with a compact B♭-minor song

sections.label: B · Piano and woodwind replies
sections.mNote: Wind phrases and a broad string melody share the second group

cues.title: The soloist accompanies
cues.text: Horns announce the opening. Then the strings sing the great D♭-major melody while the piano supplies enormous chords beneath it. The soloist makes a spectacular entrance as an accompanist.
cues.evidence: Tonic Chord’s score analysis identifies the horn opening, the string theme in bars 7–16 and the piano’s chordal accompaniment. https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano passages by force
cues.text: In December 1874, Tchaikovsky tells his brother Anatoly that he is immersed in a piano concerto. The keyboard writing is resisting him: he has to “compel piano passages to come into my head”.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Anatoly Tchaikovsky, letter 372, 21 November/3 December 1874. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: A smaller, sharper tune
cues.text: The Allegro con spirito begins in B♭ minor with a short Ukrainian tune. Its clipped phrases replace the introduction’s long string melody; the piano turns the song into quick, insistent exchanges with the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Allegro theme and its Ukrainian source: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1. Exposition and piano–orchestra exchanges: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A singer in Ukraine
cues.text: The Allegro’s tune comes from a blind street singer Tchaikovsky hears in Ukraine. In a letter to Nadezhda von Meck in May 1879, he remembers the singer’s accompanying instrument and says he uses part of the melody in this concerto.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Nadezhda von Meck, letter 1174, 6/18–13/25 May 1879, quoted under Related Works. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Rubinstein says no
cues.text: On 5 January 1875, Tchaikovsky plays the concerto to Nikolay Rubinstein and Nikolay Hubert. Rubinstein condemns it and asks for changes. Tchaikovsky refuses. Hans von Bülow eventually takes the new work to Boston.
cues.evidence: The private play-through is recounted in Tchaikovsky’s letter 736 to Nadezhda von Meck, 2–3 February 1878. Date, participants and Boston première: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1.

cues.title: Tunes caught in the octaves
cues.text: The development moves the earlier tunes through new keys. Piano octaves break across the orchestra; short pieces of the first subject interrupt the more lyrical phrases. The grand introductory melody stays outside this argument.
cues.evidence: First-movement development, octave writing and thematic plan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky); https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Ukrainian tune returns
cues.text: The Allegro’s first tune returns in shortened form. Tchaikovsky then revisits the wind melody and rebuilds the earlier climax, this time towards B♭ major.
cues.evidence: The shortened first-subject return and B♭-major recapitulation climax are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano has the room
cues.text: The orchestra stops for the long cadenza. The pianist brings earlier melodies into the solo writing, eventually recalling the wind theme quietly in B♭ minor.
cues.evidence: First-movement cadenza and its quiet B♭-minor recollection of the second-subject theme: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra answers softly
cues.text: The orchestra returns with the broad melody from the second group, now in B♭ major. After the pianist’s long solo, the tune has other players to breathe with again.
cues.evidence: Closing section after the cadenza: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky); Tonic Chord identifies the B♭-major return at bar 642, https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A B♭-major finish
cues.text: Piano and orchestra bring the Allegro’s tunes into a short, vigorous coda. The movement ends in B♭ major, with a plagal cadence: the chord of E♭ major settles onto B♭.
cues.evidence: First-movement coda and concluding plagal cadence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: D♭ major closes; B♭ minor begins
transitions.from: Intro · Piano chords beneath the strings
transitions.how: The D♭-major introduction quietens before the Allegro con spirito begins in B♭ minor. The piano takes up a short Ukrainian melody, replacing the strings’ broad tune with clipped phrases and quick exchanges.
transitions.evidence: Introduction and exposition described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky). Ukrainian source documented at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1.

transitions.title: Woodwind phrases open a second group
transitions.how: The second group alternates a woodwind theme with a smoother string melody in A♭ major. Piano arpeggios accompany the wind tune when it returns, carrying its shorter phrases into a larger orchestral build.
transitions.evidence: First-movement second-subject group, A♭-major string melody and piano arpeggios: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: The closing tune begins the development
transitions.to: Dev · Themes between piano and orchestra
transitions.how: The exposition closes in A♭ major. Its lyrical closing theme becomes a rising sequence in the development, interrupted by pieces of the first subject. Piano octaves and orchestral replies pull the familiar tunes away from their earlier keys.

transitions.title: The Allegro tune returns in shortened form
transitions.from: Dev · Themes between piano and orchestra
transitions.how: Winds and strings recover the Allegro’s first theme. Tchaikovsky shortens its return, then gives the piano octave writing on the way to the second group. The later orchestral climax turns towards B♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Recapitulation scoring and octave transformation: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/. B♭-major climax: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: A diverted cadence leaves the piano alone
transitions.how: The B♭-major climax is cut short by a deceptive cadence, which turns away from the expected home chord. The orchestra stops, leaving the pianist alone for the long cadenza. Quiet fragments of the wind theme eventually return in B♭ minor.

transitions.title: B♭ major brings the orchestra back
transitions.to: Link · The orchestra returns in B♭
transitions.how: The cadenza releases the broad second-group melody to the orchestra in B♭ major. Sustained orchestral notes rejoin the piano, and the returning tune begins the approach to the coda.
transitions.evidence: Orchestral re-entry with the second group’s lyrical theme: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: The piano drives towards B♭ major
transitions.from: Link · The orchestra returns in B♭
transitions.to: Coda · Piano and orchestra finish together
transitions.how: Piano and orchestra gather speed and force around the Allegro’s first and second themes. The brief coda ends in B♭ major with a plagal cadence, E♭ major resolving to B♭.
transitions.evidence: The coda’s themes, B♭-major close and plagal cadence are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
